paragraphs.title: Punishment for Israel’s Joy and Unfaithfulness

answers: Because Israel has gone whoring from God
easy.explanation: Israel is warned not to rejoice because it has been unfaithful to God.
easy.q: Why is Israel told not to rejoice like other nations?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “thou hast loved a reward upon every cornfloor.”
easy.q: What did Israel love upon every cornfloor?

answers: They will be given to the priests
They will not feed Israel, and the new wine will fail
easy.explanation: The floor and winepress will not provide for Israel, and the new wine will fail.
easy.q: What will happen to the floor and the winepress?

answers: Israel’s blessing will be taken away
The harvest will be given to Egypt
medium.explanation: Because of Israel’s unfaithfulness, its grain and wine will no longer sustain it.
medium.q: What connection does the passage make between Israel’s unfaithfulness and its harvest?

medium.explanation: “Reward” refers to payment or gain, associated here with the harvest.
medium.q: What does the word “reward” mean in verse 1?

answers: It will be unable to worship the LORD properly in the land
medium.explanation: Israel will not dwell in the LORD’s land and will not offer acceptable worship there.
medium.q: What additional loss will Israel suffer besides the loss of crops?

answers: Sin affects both provision and worship
challenge.explanation: The passage connects the loss of food and wine with the loss of proper worship in the land.
challenge.q: What does the movement from the cornfloor and winepress to the LORD’s land emphasize?

answers: Israel will live outside the holy setting of the LORD’s land
Israel will enjoy a feast at the temple
Israel will receive food from the priests
challenge.explanation: Exile in Assyria means Israel will eat outside the proper holy order of the LORD’s land.
challenge.q: What does eating unclean things in Assyria signify?

answers: Rejoicing, prosperity, and dwelling in the land
Unfaithfulness, failed crops, exile, and rejected worship
challenge.explanation: Israel’s unfaithfulness leads to failed provision, exile, and the loss of acceptable worship.
challenge.q: Which sequence best summarizes the punishment in these verses?

paragraphs.title: The Days of Calamity and Exile

easy.explanation: The prophet asks, “What will ye do in the solemn day, and in the day of the feast of the LORD?”
easy.q: What question is asked about the solemn day and the day of the feast?

answers: Egypt and other lands of exile
easy.explanation: The passage says they are gone because of destruction, and Egypt shall gather them up.
easy.q: Where will Israel go because of destruction?

answers: Nettles and thorns will possess them
easy.explanation: Nettles will possess their pleasant places, and thorns will be in their tabernacles.
easy.q: What will happen to their pleasant places and tabernacles?

answers: They will become associated with destruction and judgment
The feast will last only one day
medium.explanation: The prophet asks what Israel will do on the feast day because calamity and judgment are coming.
medium.q: Why are the feast days not presented as ordinary days of joy?

medium.explanation: “Hatred” describes the hostility directed toward the prophet and the house of God.
medium.q: What does “hatred” mean in this passage?

answers: By calling the prophet a fool and the spiritual man mad
By asking the prophet to lead the feast
medium.explanation: Israel rejects the message, calling the prophet a fool and the spiritual man mad.
medium.q: How does Israel regard the prophet’s message?

answers: Exile leaves their places abandoned and exposes them to destruction
Their possessions allow them to remain in the land
Their possessions protect them from judgment
challenge.explanation: As the people depart, their places are left to nettles and thorns, showing the effects of exile.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the loss of possessions and exile?

answers: Rejection and contempt for his message
challenge.explanation: The insult shows that Israel despises the prophet and refuses to heed his warning.
challenge.q: What does the title “the prophet is a fool” reveal about Israel’s attitude?

answers: Rejection of the prophet, ignored judgment, destruction, and exile
Acceptance of the prophet, prosperity, and restoration
Feast, harvest, and cancellation of exile
challenge.explanation: Israel rejects the warning, but the days of visitation and destruction still arrive.
challenge.q: Which cause-and-effect sequence best fits these verses?

paragraphs.title: Deepening Sin and the Memory of the Past

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah.”
easy.q: To what days is Israel’s corruption compared?

easy.explanation: God will remember their iniquity and visit their sins.
easy.q: What will God do concerning Israel’s iniquity and sins?

answers: Like grapes in the wilderness and the firstripe in the fig tree
easy.explanation: God found Israel like grapes in the wilderness and saw its fathers as the first ripe fig.
easy.q: How did God first describe finding Israel?

answers: Israel was precious to God but turned to Baal-peor
Israel was exiled but returned home
Israel was poor but became wealthy
medium.explanation: Israel was once precious to God, but it went to Baal-peor and became abominable.
medium.q: What is the central contrast in these verses?

answers: They devoted themselves to a shameful idol
medium.explanation: The phrase describes Israel’s devotion to the shameful worship of Baal-peor.
medium.q: What does “separated themselves unto that shame” mean?

answers: To show that present corruption repeats an earlier pattern of sin
medium.explanation: The comparison with Gibeah shows that Israel’s corruption follows a recurring pattern.
medium.q: Why does the passage recall Israel’s earlier history?

answers: God regarded Israel as precious and desirable
Israel always lived in the wilderness
Israel had no relationship with God
challenge.explanation: Grapes found in a wilderness suggest something rare, valuable, and greatly appreciated.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the image of grapes in the wilderness?

answers: Israel’s misplaced love led it away from God
Baal-peor was a servant of God
challenge.explanation: Israel’s love for Baal-peor resulted in separation from God and spiritual shame.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between going to Baal-peor and being loved show?

answers: Persistent corruption brings remembered and punished sin
The visitation concerns only good deeds
challenge.explanation: The passage links Israel’s deep corruption with God’s remembering and judging its sins.
challenge.q: How are deep corruption and the visitation of sin related?

paragraphs.title: The Loss of the Future and the Sorrow of Children

answers: It will fly away like a bird
easy.explanation: Ephraim’s glory will fly away like a bird.
easy.q: What will happen to Ephraim’s glory?

answers: They will serve in the temple
easy.explanation: The passage says, “Though they bring up their children, yet will I bereave them.”
easy.q: What will happen to Ephraim’s children?

answers: A miscarrying womb and dry breasts
easy.explanation: The prophet asks for “a miscarrying womb and dry breasts.”
easy.q: What does the prophet ask the LORD to give them?

answers: The loss will affect life from its earliest beginning
The loss will occur only in old age
The children will leave when grown
medium.explanation: These phrases emphasize that the judgment reaches back to conception, birth, and the womb.
medium.q: What is emphasized by the words “from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception”?

answers: A womb unable to carry a child successfully
A womb belonging only to an elderly woman
medium.explanation: The expression refers to a womb that cannot bring a pregnancy to a successful birth.
medium.q: What does “a miscarrying womb” mean in context?

answers: As planted in a pleasant place
As a people without a history
As already scattered among all nations
medium.explanation: Ephraim is described as planted in a pleasant place, suggesting former prosperity.
medium.q: How is Ephraim described before its judgment is announced?

answers: Both express the collapse of Ephraim’s future and continuity
challenge.explanation: The departure of glory and the loss of children together portray the destruction of Ephraim’s future.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the loss of glory and the loss of children?

answers: Ephraim once appeared established and prosperous
Ephraim always lived beside the sea
challenge.explanation: Being planted in a pleasant place pictures stability, fertility, and former prosperity.
challenge.q: What does the image of Ephraim planted in a pleasant place suggest?

answers: To express judgment on both childbirth and the nurturing of children
To describe the wealth of the land
challenge.explanation: The womb represents birth, while dry breasts represent the inability to nourish children.
challenge.q: Why does the prophet mention both the womb and the breasts?

paragraphs.title: The Rejection and Expulsion of Ephraim

easy.explanation: The verse says, “All their wickedness is in Gilgal.”
easy.q: Where is all their wickedness said to be?

answers: Dried up and unable to bear fruit
easy.explanation: Ephraim is smitten, its root is dried up, and it shall bear no fruit.
The final verse says they shall be wanderers among the nations.
easy.q: What will be Ephraim’s condition among the nations?

answers: Expulsion from God’s house and the end of His love
Return to the land and blessing
medium.explanation: Because of their wickedness, God will drive them out of His house and love them no more.
medium.q: What will result from the wickedness committed at Gilgal?

answers: They have lost the basis for fruitful and continuing life
medium.explanation: A dried root represents the loss of vitality, stability, and fruitfulness.
medium.q: What does “their root is dried up” mean figuratively?

answers: Both show Ephraim’s rejection and loss of stability
Fruitlessness leads to prosperity among the nations
Wandering helps Ephraim become firmly rooted
medium.explanation: Ephraim’s lack of fruit and wandering both express its rejection and loss of a secure home.
medium.q: How are fruitlessness and wandering related?

answers: The image moves from lack of fruitfulness to loss of place and stability
It describes a return from exile
challenge.explanation: The dried root pictures lifelessness, while wandering pictures the loss of land and stability.
challenge.q: What is the significance of moving from a dried root to wandering among the nations?

answers: Expulsion from God’s house leads to life among foreign peoples
challenge.explanation: Being driven out of God’s house results in exile and wandering among the nations.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between being driven out of God’s house and wandering among the nations?

answers: Because they did not hearken unto him
challenge.explanation: The verse directly states that God will cast them away because they did not listen to Him.
challenge.q: According to the final verse, why will God cast Ephraim away?
